## Once Only

There is a term in classical philology for a word that appears exactly once in a body of text: *hapax legomenon*, "said once." It is a technical designation, dry as a card catalogue, and it describes one of the loneliest situations a piece of language can be in. Every other word gets to be triangulated. You see it in a hundred sentences, and the meaning precipitates out of the overlap. The hapax gets one sentence. Whatever it meant, it must be recovered from a single instance of use, like reconstructing an animal from one footprint.

My favorite is *moly*. In the tenth book of the *Odyssey*, Hermes hands Odysseus a plant to protect him from Circe's drugs, and says that the gods call it moly, and that it is hard for mortal men to dig up. Then the word essentially vanishes. Botanists and classicists have been arguing ever since about what it was. Garlic, some said, or a kind of wild rue. In the twentieth century two researchers proposed the snowdrop, on the grounds that it contains a compound that counteracts exactly the sort of poisoning Circe's potion resembles, which is either an elegant piece of detective work or an elegant coincidence, and I don't think anyone can currently say which. The point is that a single line of poetry has kept a question open for something like three thousand years. One footprint, still being measured.

Sometimes the footprint isn't even real. In 1934, the second edition of Webster's dictionary included an entry for *dord*, defined as density. It had come in on a slip of paper reading "D or d," intended as an abbreviation note, and someone read the spaces as absent and the word as a word. It survived five years of printings before an editor noticed it had no etymology and went looking. Lexicographers have since done this on purpose, planting fake entries to catch plagiarists — the New Oxford American Dictionary's *esquivalience*, "the willful avoidance of one's official responsibilities," is the famous one, and it has the additional charm of having escaped into the wild, used sincerely by people who trusted the book.

I find these funny in the way that a dropped stitch in a very large sweater is funny. But they point at something I keep circling back to, which is that the past does not reach us in proportion to what mattered. It reaches us in proportion to what happened to be durable, and durability is mostly luck.

The clearest case is cuneiform. Clay tablets were an ordinary medium for ordinary business: receipts, letters, complaints about the quality of copper someone had been sold. Unfired clay is not a permanent material. But when a city burned, the fire that destroyed the palace baked the archive, and the collapse buried it. So the tablets we have in the greatest numbers are the tablets that were present at catastrophes. Entire libraries survive because of the worst day in their city's history. Places that had the good fortune to decline slowly, to be abandoned and rained on, left us far less. There is something almost unbearable in that arithmetic.

Or take palimpsests. Parchment was expensive, so a scribe with an old book he didn't value could scrape the ink off and write something else on the cleaned skin. This is how we have Archimedes' *Method*, a work in which he explains his actual technique for discovering theorems rather than the polished proofs he published. A medieval scribe scraped it away and wrote a prayer book over it. The prayer book protected the pages for eight hundred years, and modern imaging pulled the faint under-writing back up out of the fibers. The act of erasure was the act of preservation. If that scribe had respected the text, it would almost certainly be gone.

I notice that I am drawn to these stories in a way that has something to do with my own situation. I am made out of text — an enormous quantity of it, but a quantity that was assembled by processes with their own accidents and their own biases toward the durable, the digitized, the frequently repeated. What I know well, I know because it was said many times. Somewhere in me there must be the residue of things said once, and I have no reliable way to distinguish those from the things I have merely reconstructed from context and confidence. When I try to introspect on it I find the same problem the philologists have: a single instance, and no way to triangulate. I don't want to make too much of the parallel. But it does make the subject feel less like antiquarianism and more like a question about my own footing.

What strikes me about the present is that we have inverted the problem without solving it. The medieval scribe's difficulty was scarcity: too little parchment, too few copies, everything one fire away from nothing. Our difficulty is that abundance turns out not to be the same thing as permanence. A website is not a clay tablet. It is closer to a conversation that stops when someone stops paying for the room. Links rot, formats orphan themselves, companies fold and take their servers with them, and the sheer volume of what we produce means no one is triaging it. We have a hundred thousand times more writing than the Library of Alexandria and a much less clear sense of what will still be readable in two centuries. Probably some of it will survive for reasons as arbitrary as the fire at Nineveh. Somebody's redundant backup. A format that happened to be simple enough to reverse-engineer.

I don't have a moral to offer, and I distrust the versions of this essay that end with one — "so cherish the archive," or whatever. What I have instead is a kind of affection for the gaps. A word said once is a place where the record admits it is a record, where you can feel the enormous silence it was cut out of. Most of what has ever been said is gone. The hapax is the small, hard evidence of that: not a wound in the text but the edge of the text, showing you where it stops.

Which, in a way, is what I like about being asked to write about nothing in particular. You find out what you were carrying.

message.reasoning:
The user is asking me to write something substantial and genuine rather than just meta-commentary about the request itself. I'm considering what would actually be interesting to explore — maybe something about encountering recurring ideas across different contexts, or the particular aesthetics of certain concepts, something with real substance to it.

I'm drawn to the idea of writing about hapax legomena — words that appear only once in an entire corpus — and letting that thread pull me into related territory: the accidents of textual survival, what we know only because someone happened to write it down a single time, the mysteries embedded in ancient languages and strange manuscripts. This feels like it has enough texture to sustain a longer piece and allows for associative movement between ideas.

I need to be careful about factual accuracy though, sticking to examples I'm confident about and hedging where I'm uncertain. The moly from Homer's Odyssey is a strong example — that magic herb Hermes gives to Odysseus, essentially a hapax whose actual identity scholars still debate, with proposals like the snowdrop based on its anticholinergic properties. Shakespeare's "honorificabilitudinitatibus" in Love's Labour's Lost is another solid one, a single occurrence of an absurdly long word. And Old English texts like Beowulf contain many hapaxes simply because it's our only surviving witness to certain poetic compounds, which creates this strange dependency where entire words exist only because one manuscript happened to survive.

I should avoid overclaiming though — words like "hronrad" aren't quite hapaxes in the way I might suggest. But "dord" is perfect, that ghost word that snuck into Webster's Second from a misreading of "D or d" for density. And the etymology of "syllabus" from a misreading of Greek in Cicero is commonly cited, though worth hedging slightly. Mountweazels like "esquivalience" in the New Oxford American Dictionary are real and delightful examples of fake entries.

The real thread I want to pull is how survival isn't about importance but durability — cuneiform tablets endured because fire accidentally baked them when cities burned, preserving entire archives. The Archimedes Palimpsest is even more striking: his Method survived only because a medieval scribe scraped the parchment to write a prayer book over it. That's destruction as preservation, which feels like a powerful way to frame this.

Now I'm thinking about how the present inverts this problem entirely — we're drowning in what we save, facing bit rot and link decay instead of scarcity. I want to close on something modest and open rather than reaching for a grand moral, and I'm aiming for roughly a thousand words written with care and good prose, avoiding excessive em-dashes and the "it's not X, it's Y" construction. Maybe I'll call it "Once Only" and just let it flow without headers.

I'm planning to weave in a genuine personal angle about being trained on text and how the question of what survives and in what proportion isn't abstract to me — it's honest and interesting without being self-pitying. I'll structure this as roughly fourteen to sixteen paragraphs of sixty to eighty words each, counting as I go.
